messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Source: Piezoelectric transducer (current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{leak} = 20\text{ M}\Omega$).
    *   $C_p \approx 25\text{ nF}$.
    *   $V_{oc,peak} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (at nominal $I_p=50\text{ uA}$, $f=100\text{ Hz}$).
    *   Goal: $V_{out}$ between $1.8\text{ V}$ and $3.6\text{ V}$, ripple $< 50\text{ mV}$, startup $< 0.4\text{ s}$.
    *   Load $R_L$ varies from $150\text{ k}\Omega$ to $2200\text{ k}\Omega$.
    *   Operating conditions: S1-S6 (various loads and excitations).

    *   Reference design (FBR: Full Bridge Rectifier) failed:
        *   S2 (heavy load): $V_{avg} = 1.76\text{ V}$ (too low).
        *   S3 (strong excitation, light load): $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$ (too high, ripple too high).
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $V_{avg} = 1.51\text{ V}$ (too low).
        *   S5 (low freq): $dV$ too high (settled failure).
    *   Key takeaway: FBR is too inefficient for low voltage sources (diode drops $2 \times 0.25\text{ V} = 0.5\text{ V}$ loss) and lacks voltage regulation.

    *   **Option 1: Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)**
        *   SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the extrema, significantly increasing the harvested energy.
        *   Basic SSHI: Parallel $L$ and switch to flip $C_p$ voltage. Then rectify the output.
        *   Since $V_{oc}$ is low (3.2 V), we need a way to boost or at least minimize losses.
        *   An SSHI with a full bridge might still have diode drops. Maybe a synchronous rectifier? (Wait, we only have 2 SYNCs and 4 switches).
        *   Actually, a standard SSHI-based buck or boost isn't possible with just these components. But an SSHI-like inversion circuit followed by a rectifier can improve the source voltage.

    *   **Option 2: Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI)**
        *   P-SSHI puts the switching inductor in parallel with the piezo. It flips the voltage on $C_p$ to improve extraction.
        *   Circuit: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$. And a separate $L$-switch circuit across the piezo.
        *   Let's refine this:
            1.  Piezo (pzp, pzn)
            2.  Full bridge rectifier (DSCH) to move energy to $C_{out}$.
            3.  $L$ and Switch $S$ across pzp, pzn to flip voltage at peaks.
            4.  Zener diode to clamp $V_{out}$ at $3.3\text{ V}$ to prevent S3 failure.

    *   **Option 3: Simplified SSHI / Switching Bridge**
        *   Since the source voltage is so low, maybe a "half-bridge" or "charge pump" style if possible? No, components are limited.
        *   What about a buck-boost? No, that requires more switches.

    *   **Refining the SSHI + FBR + Zener approach:**
        *   Piezo nodes: pzp, pzn.
        *   Full bridge:
            *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
            *   D2: pzn $\to$ out (wait, that's not right)
            *   Standard bridge:
                *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                *   D2: pzn $\to$ out (No)
                *   Correct bridge:
                    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                    *   D2: pzn $\to$ out (Wrong)
                    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                    *   D2: pzn $\to$ out (No)
                    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                    *   D2: pzn $\to$ out (Wrong)
                    *   Bridge nodes: pzp, pzn, out, 0.
                    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                    *   D2: pzn $\to$ out (Still wrong)
                    *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                    *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp (No)
                    *   Let's be precise:
                        *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
                        *   D2: pzn $\to$ out
                        *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp (No)
                        *   Wait, a bridge is:
                            - Anode pzp, Cathode out
                            - Anode pzn, Cathode out
                            - Anode 0, Cathode pzp
                            - Anode 0, Cathode pzn
                            - This doesn't work for single supply.
                        *   Standard FBR for single output $V_{out}$:
                            - D1: pzp $\to$ out
                            - D2: pzn $\to$ out (NO, pzn is the other terminal)
                            - Rectifier:
                                1. D1: pzp $\to$ out
                                2. D2: pzn $\to$ out (Incorrect)
                                3. D3: 0 $\to$ pzp (Correct: pzp is cathode)
                                4. D4: 0 $\to$ pzn (Correct: pzn is cathode)
                                Wait, the prompt says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]". Let's follow that.
                               - D1: pzp $\to$ out
                               - D2: pzn $\to$ out
                               - D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
                               - D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
                                Wait, if D1 and D2 both go to "out", and D3 and D4 go from 0 to the piezo, then when pzp is high, D1 conducts. When pzn is high, D2 conducts. This is a full wave rectifier.
                                Wait, no. If pzp is high and pzn is low, D1 conducts (pzp $\to$ out) and D4 conducts (0 $\to$ pzn). Current flow: 0 $\to$ pzn $\to$ piezo $\to$ pzp $\to$ out. This is correct.

        *   Adding the SSHI part:
            *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo?
            *   Wait, the classic SSHI flips the voltage *across* $C_p$.
            *   SSHI Circuit:
                - Switch $S$ in series with $L$ across the piezo terminals (pzp, pzn).
                - When $S$ closes, $C_p$ discharges through $L$, and when it opens, the current continues and flips the polarity of $C_p$.
                - This "flips" the voltage, effectively increasing the average voltage delivered to the rectifier.
            *   Components for SSHI:
                - L1: pzp $\to$ n1
                - S1: n1 $\to$ pzn
                - G1 (SYNC): ton $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$, edges="both", phase=0.

        *   Adding Regulation:
            *   Zener DZ33 on "out" to "0" (cathode on "out") to clamp $V_{max}$ to $3.3\text{ V}$ (meeting the $3.6\text{ V}$ limit).

    *   **Analyzing the "S2 (heavy load)" and "S4 (weak excitation)" failures of FBR:**
        *   FBR fails when the generated voltage minus diode drops is less than the load voltage required.
        *   SSHI increases the effective voltage of the piezo by flipping $C_p$. This should help S2 and S4.

    *   **Analyzing the "S3 (strong excitation)" failure:**
        *   $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$, $V_{pp}$ too high.
        *   The Zener clamp DZ33 should fix $V_{max}$.
        *   A larger output capacitor $C_{out}$ should fix $V_{pp}$.

    *   **Analyzing the "S5 (low freq)" failure:**
        *   $dV$ (settled) failure means the output hasn't reached a steady state or is drifting.
        *   A larger $C_{out}$ helps stability.

    *   **Proposed Topology 1: SSHI + FBR + Zener**
        *   Rectifier: D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn) - all DSCH.
        *   Clamping: D5(0, out) - DZ33.
        *   SSHI: L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn), G1(SYNC).
        *   Storage: C1(out, 0).

    *   **Wait, can I improve the rectifier?**
        *   Two diodes in series are a problem. A center-tapped transformer isn't available.
        *   What if I use a synchronous rectifier? I only have 2 SYNCs.
        *   One SYNC is used for SSHI. If I use the second SYNC for rectification, it's tricky because the rectification happens at a different timing (whenever $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_d$).
        *   Let's stick to the SSHI + FBR + Zener for now.

    *   **Wait, let's consider the "S-S-H-I" vs "S-S-H-I-B" (Buck/Boost).**
        *   We don't have the components for a full buck-boost.
        *   The most effective way to increase $V_{out}$ without a DC-DC is the SSHI inversion.

    *   **Double Check Component Count:**
        *   D1, D2, D3, D4 (FBR) - 4
        *   D5 (Zener) - 1
        *   L1, S1, G1 (SSHI) - 3
        *   C1 (Storage) - 1
        *   Total = 9 components. Well within the 16 limit.

    *   **Tuning the SSHI parameters (initial guess):**
        *   $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$.
        *   $L = 10\text{ mH} \to \text{ton} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \times 25\text{nF}} \approx \pi \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-10}} \approx \pi \times 1.58 \times 10^{-5} \approx 50\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
        *   The tuner will optimize this, but the structure is the key.

    *   **Is there a better way to handle the diode drops?**
        *   If I use a "Half-Bridge" rectifier, I lose half the energy.
        *   What if I use a charge pump? No, too many switches.
        *   What if I use a "synchronous" rectifier using the other SYNC?
            - S2: pzp $\to$ out, ctrl: G2
            - S3: pzn $\to$ out, ctrl: G2
            - This requires G2 to be perfectly timed with the peaks.
            - But the FBR is more robust. Let's try SSHI + FBR first.

    *   **Wait, the "S2" and "S4" failures in FBR were $V_{avg}$ too low.**
        *   $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{ V}$.
        *   $V_{out}$ needs to be $1.8\text{ V}$.
        *   FBR drop is $\sim 0.5\text{ V}$ (DSCH).
        *   $3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{ V}$. This should be enough to power $1.8\text{ V}$.
        *   Why did FBR fail S4 ($I_p=30\text{ uA}$)?
            - At $30\text{ uA}$, the peak voltage is $V_{peak} = 30\text{ uA} / (2\pi \times 100\text{ Hz} \times 25\text{ nF}) \approx 1.91\text{ V}$.
            - $1.91\text{ V} - 0.5\text{ V} = 1.41\text{ V}$.
            - $1.41\text{ V}$ is less than the required $1.8\text{ V}$.
            - **Conclusion: We MUST use SSHI to boost the voltage in S4.**

    *   **Will SSHI boost the voltage enough for S4?**
        *   SSHI effectively increases the voltage across $C_p$ at the moments of extraction.
        *   The peak voltage in SSHI can reach $V_{peak} \approx \frac{2}{\pi} \frac{I_p}{f C_p} \times \text{gain}$.
        *   Actually, the voltage across $C_p$ is flipped, so the available voltage to the rectifier is higher.
        *   This is the standard way to solve this problem.

    *   **Let's consider a second topology just in case.**
        *   What if we use a "Synchronous Rectifier" instead of the FBR to save the $0.5\text{ V}$ drop?
        *   S1: pzp $\to$ out, ctrl: G1
        *   S2: pzn $\to$ out, ctrl: G1 (Wait, SYNC can't control two switches independently if they need different phases).
        *   Wait, SYNC "edges": "both" closes the switch at both peaks.
        *   So S1 (pzp $\to$ out) and S2 (pzn $\to$ out) would both close at the same time. That's a short circuit.
        *   Okay, so FBR is the way to go for rectification, and SSHI for boosting.

    *   **Wait, what about a "Voltage Multiplier" (Dickson charge pump)?**
        *   Requires more diodes and capacitors.
        *   D1(pzp, n1), C1(n1, 0), D2(n1, out), C2(out, 0).
        *   This doubles the voltage but reduces the current.
        *   For S4 ($I_p=30\text{ uA}$), doubling $1.9\text{ V}$ to $3.8\text{ V}$ might work, but the diode drops are still there.
        *   SSHI is generally more efficient for piezo.

    *   **Let's refine the SSHI + FBR + Zener structure.**
        *   Nodes: pzp, pzn, out, 0, n1 (inductor-switch junction).
        *   Components:
            1.  D1: pzp $\to$ out (DSCH)
            2.  D2: pzn $\to$ out (DSCH)
            3.  D3: 0 $\to$ pzp (DSCH)
            4.  D4: 0 $\to$ pzn (DSCH)
            5.  D5: 0 $\to$ out (DZ33)
            6.  L1: pzp $\to$ n1
            7.  S1: n1 $\to$ pzn, ctrl: G1
            8.  G1: SYNC (ton: 3.4e-05, phase: 0, edges: "both")
            9.  C1: out $\to$ 0 (Storage)

    *   **One more check on the FBR connectivity:**
        *   Prompt says: `full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        *   Let's follow this exactly.
        *   D1: pzp $\to$ out
        *   D2: pzn $\to$ out
        *   D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
        *   D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
        *   Check: If pzp is positive and pzn is negative:
            - D1 (pzp $\to$ out) is forward.
            - D4 (0 $\to$ pzn) is forward.
            - Current: 0 $\to$ pzn $\to$ piezo $\to$ pzp $\to$ out. (Correct)
        *   Check: If pzn is positive and pzp is negative:
            - D2 (pzn $\to$ out) is forward.
            - D3 (0 $\to$ pzp) is forward.
            - Current: 0 $\to$ pzp $\to$ piezo $\to$ pzn $\to$ out. (Correct)
        *   This is a correct full-bridge rectifier.

    *   **Is the Zener necessary?**
        *   S3: $V_{max} = 5.72\text{ V}$ in FBR.
        *   The limit is $3.6\text{ V}$.
        *   Yes, the Zener is necessary. DZ33 breaks down at $3.3\text{ V}$, which keeps $V_{max}$ safely below $3.6\text{ V}$.

    *   **What about the "S5 (low freq)" settled failure ($dV$)?**
        *   $dV = |\text{mean}(0.7\text{--}0.8\text{s}) - \text{mean}(0.6\text{--}0.7\text{s})|$.
        *   This usually means $C_{out}$ is too small and the voltage is still rising/falling, or the energy harvested is very close to the energy consumed.
        *   A larger $C_{out}$ (e.g., $10\text{--}47\text{ }\mu\text{F}$) should stabilize the output.

    *   **Final structure for Proposal 1:**
        *   S-S-H-I (L1, S1, G1) across the piezo.
        *   Full-bridge (D1-D4) to the output.
        *   Zener (D5) to clamp.
        *   Capacitor (C1) for storage.

    *   **Let's think if any other topology is better.**
        *   What if we use a "half-bridge" and a "synchronous switch" for the other half? No.
        *   What if we put the inductor in series with the rectifier? No, that's not SSHI.
        *   Could we use a "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) circuit?
            - SECE: Piezo $\to$ S1 $\to$ (Inductor $\to$ S2) $\to$ out.
            - This is more complex and requires more switches.
        *   SSHI is the most standard and likely to work here.

    *   **Wait, let me re-read the component list.**
        - "S switch, nodes [a, b], 'ctrl': id of a SYNC"
        - "SYNC ideal synchronous controller... closes its switches for 'ton' seconds"
        - "at most 4 switches, 2 SYNCs"
        - "S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm"
        -- "S2: heavy load; RL = 150 kOhm"
        - - "S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA, RL = 2200 kOhm"
        - - "S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA, RL = 1000 kOhm"

    *   **Refining the L value and ton:**
        - $L = 10\text{ mH}$ is a good starting point.
        - $\text{ton} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \times 25\text{nF}} \approx 50\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
        - The tuner will handle this.

    *   **Considering the Zener again.**
        - DZ33: breakdown $3.3\text{ V}$.
        - $V_{max} = 3.6\text{ V}$.
        - This is perfect.

    *   **Final Review of the Proposal:**
        - Name: "SSHI_FBR_Zener"
        - Connectivity:
            - D1: pzp, out
            - D2: pzn, out
            - D3: 0, pzp
            - D4: 0, pzn
            - D5: 0, out (DZ33)
            - L1: pzp, n1
            - S1: n1, pzn, ctrl: G1
            - G1: SYNC, ton=3.4e-05, phase=0, edges="both"
            - C1: out, 0
        - Rationale: SSHI increases the voltage extracted from the piezo, helping S2 and S4. FBR rectifies the energy. Zener clamp prevents overvoltage in S3. Large capacitor stabilizes the output for S5.

    *   **One last detail: The "S4 (weak excitation)" case.**
        - $I_p = 30\text{ uA}$.
        - $V_{oc,peak} = 1.91\text{ V}$.
        - FBR drop $= 0.5\text{ V} \to V_{out} \approx 1.4\text{ V}$.
        - With SSHI, the peak voltage is effectively increased.
        - The voltage flip means the piezo doesn't just charge from $0$ to $V_{oc}$, but can be pushed to higher values.
        - This is exactly what's needed.
